items.title: Everybody hates Pat McAfee
items.content:
here’s an election next week, which means that you and I are currently being bombarded, ceaselessly, with unwanted voices. Here’s one such voice that, alas, we cannot vote out of office come Tuesday:

That’s ESPN commentator and one-man pandemic Pat McAfee. If you’re unfamiliar with McAfee’s work, I envy you. No seriously, if I could trade bodies with you right now, I’d do it in a heartbeat. I don’t even care if you’re 85 and dying of gonorrhea, I’d still do it. That’s just how much I can’t stand Pat McAfee.

Article continues below this ad

And I’m hardly alone. The clip you see up above is McAfee’s response to the harassment (NOTE: term used with ultimate generosity) he endured before co-hosting “College GameDay” for the four-letter live from the Salt Lake City campus of the University of Utah this past Saturday. McAfee is a known quantity to college football fans by now. They know that he’s the former Indianapolis Colts punter who abruptly retired from pro football to take a job for the chauvinist liberation front that is Barstool Sports. They know that McAfee parlayed his Barstool gig into a high-profile radio show where he paid Steelers QB and emotional cancer Aaron Rodgers literal millions of dollars to come on the air with him to muse at length about the dangers of getting vaccinated. And they know that ESPN, desperate to appeal to teenage gambling addicts, scooped up McAfee to become the de facto face of their network, now to the tune of $60 million a year.

They also know that McAfee absolutely, unequivocally sucks.

That’s why, prior to McAfee’s arrival in SLC on Saturday, a few Utah students made a short video of Utes fans doing their best McAfee impressions, which the university found harmless enough to post to its Instagram account (since deleted). I cannot stress how gentle of a ribbing McAfee gets in this video. Even Mitt Romney thinks these kids could have gone in harder on him. But McAfee himself found the video incredibly distressing, so much so that he told his studio bros afterward that he feared for his life going into the belly of the beast!

Article continues below this ad

“The university puts that out? Like as I’m about to go out and do an infomercial for the place? And then I’m walking in front of thousands of these people. This is how the university feels about it? It’s an uncomfortable feeling … I thought to myself, has anything, like, really scary happened at a college gathering in the state of Utah recently?”

McAfee there is referring to the late Charlie Kirk, who was fatally shot while on stage at a campus event at Utah Valley University over a year ago. For reference, the UVU campus is located some 40 miles away from Salt Lake. So why would McAfee instantly think of Kirk getting killed right after a handful of mean and nasty college kids taunted him for always taking his shirt off? Well it’s because, like Kirk, McAfee is a self-absorbed asshole.

Article continues below this ad

And even more galling than McAfee’s inability to tolerate low-ABV jokes from a bunch of Utahns is the fact that ESPN took his security risk comments at face value:

“The safety and security of our on-air team, crew and fans is paramount at ‘College GameDay.’ We are committed to ensuring a safe environment, and given the very real threats that members of our team face, we take issues involving their safety seriously. We support Pat and recognize the very real and valid concerns he has around safety and security.”

According to a report in Front Office Sports, the network apparently feared for McAfee’s safety on the road immediately after Kirk had been shot dead, and the FBI even advised McAfee to wear a bulletproof vest afterward. Although one supposes that McAfee would have simply torn that vest off while on the air to brandish a couple of “guns” of his own.

But even if McAfee was justified to feel skittish about appearing in public crowds, it’s pretty telling how ESPN responded to his concerns with such an outlandish show of force. Because what’s so valid about this man’s safety concerns compared with the concerns of the women he works with, or the women he’s endangered? Are they more valid than the VERY real safety concerns of “GameDay” field reporter Holly Rowe, who was the subject of an AI-generated video of University of Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian punching her in the face ... a video that future fifth-round pick Arch Manning openly laughed about at an official UT presser? Or Mary Kate Cornett, that Ole Miss freshman? After McAfee slandered her on the air to an oblivious Adam Schefter, Cornett’s home was swatted, with armed police knocking down her door. Were either Cornett or Rowe afforded the institutional, DEFCON 1 level response that McAfee got from ESPN (and from the University of Utah!)? Of course they didn’t. That’s because they’re women, and because ESPN didn’t pay either of them $60 million a year to be professionally unfunny 20 hours a day. Even in Donald Trump’s America, the injustice on display is blinding.

Article continues below this ad

There will be no consequences for McAfee from all this. “College GameDay” has enjoyed record ratings since he joined the program (I’d argue this is because college football, not Pat McAfee, is more popular than ever), and ESPN already stood by McAfee in the wake of the Cornett scandal. As far as that network is concerned, there’s big money to be had in cheap trolling. It’s why they pay Stephen A. Smith millions of dollars a year too, after all.

And so, you and I must bear witness to yet another unremarkable man in Pat McAfee failing upward while also clumsily making a martyr of himself. This whiny tank top will never be held accountable for his worst offenses, and he’ll always be shielded by the empty suits working above him. The whole thing is an insult to my intelligence and yours. And I already get my intelligence insulted on a daily basis in this country. Do I really need it from ESPN, too? I’m just trying to watch some football without some wildly self-absorbed, MAGA-coded jackass constantly trying to reach through the TV to suck my brains out. And yet ESPN can’t even afford me, or a handful of clever kids in Utah, that basic courtesy. So I hope that every other “GameDay” crowd from here on out makes Pat McAfee even more uncomfortable than he already is. After all, it’s only fair to return the favor.

Hearst, the parent company of SFGATE, owns 18% of ESPN.
